$AAOI earnings:

- $1B-$1.5B LTA disclosed with a hyperscaler customer

- 2nd LTA coming soon, worth 5x+ more (implying $5B-$7.5B), in its final stages. 

This LTA explicitly includes lasers, very material for AOI that they're moving to supplying merchant lasers. 

- "The demand is exceptional, unprecedented. I do not know what kind of superlatives to use to describe the amount of demand that we are seeing out there in the industry"

Yeah this commentary doesn't sound like any optical demand would slowed down if it's "exceptional + unprecedented" 

- Rejected hyperscaler slowdowns from political changes with little effect. 

- AOI Can only meet 80% of demand, in case there's a kind of reduction, the demand would be bigger than AOI future capacity

- Moving toward other financing methods than ATMs (thank god), US bank loans similar to what $NBIS is doing, I'd argue is positive, given FCF coming in later. 

- Delay in meeting capacity projections into H1 2027. $471m/month targets pushed back into H2 2027, due to electrical procurement and construction logistics, which existed before Texas governor changed. 

This part is negative part of the earnings call. To qualify this, I don't quite think hyperscalers would sign a $5-$7.5B LTA if they didn't think AOI couldn't deliver.

-  Near term Q4 guidance cut was DSP availability. AOI revised near term projections down slightly to $385M and $420M in revenue. 

Said DSP supply would ease early 2027 and that they're qualifying more suppliers. 

- Gave hiked H2 2027 capacity projections from their expansion, near term revision downward. 

- 4 to 5 ongoing UHP laser eval/quals for CPO

UHP laser segment alone would far outweigh their $3.8B MC, especially if you're executing on multi billion dollar contracts with 60%+ gross margin laseres.

TLDR:
- Long term visibility improved a lot, with est. $6-$9B cumulative LTA contracts coming soon. 
- Shift toward supplying CPO lasers merchant is fundamentally material vs. just transceivers, and what I wanted to hear
- Capacity guidance hiked into H2 2027, near term delays from electrical/DSP related procurement + installation.  

I still think we're reached peak fear levels, but wouldn't dismiss disappointing short term procurement delays + Q4 DSP bottlenecks. 

AOI likely signing an additional +$5-$7.5B in likely hyperscaler LTAs and entering merchant UHP CPO market dominanted by $LITE + $COHR. 

Factored in with the valuation drop has made medium-long term opportunities very compelling.

The 30% Nobody Calls Too Risky

One of the biggest challenges for asset managers and financial advisers today is building portfolios that match their clients’ risk profiles when cash and bonds no longer offer the protection they once did.

Some have given up on differentiated risk profiles altogether and gone 100% into equities. But how many clients would choose that allocation if they knew exactly what they were getting?

Nearly 30% of the MSCI World Index is in technology stocks, and semiconductors account for more than a third of that exposure. There’s no shortage of charts showing how large tech has become in the index. Yet most investors stay put, whether they invest through index funds or active managers.

Here’s a comparison clients rarely see: over the period measured, semiconductor stocks were more volatile than bitcoin.

Bitcoin is routinely kept out of strategic portfolios because it’s considered ‘too risky’. How often do you hear the same objection to the semiconductor exposure clients already have through a global equity fund?

Why the double standard?

Tech already drives a large part of the return of an equity-heavy portfolio, so adding more of it does little for diversification. Bitcoin’s correlation with equities, meanwhile, is lower than many investors assume. An asset can be volatile on its own and still play a role in a diversified portfolio. What matters is how much you own and how it behaves alongside everything else.

You can build multi-asset portfolios without relying on cash and bonds and still cater to different risk profiles. That starts with looking beyond the usual building blocks and asking what each investment actually contributes to the portfolio.

Infleqtion says it built 30 logical qubits from just 80 physical ones and is targeting 100 by 2028 which is the same milestone as IBM’s DOE-backed program. 

The company believes that could be enough to make quantum computing genuinely useful.

quoted.text:
INFLEQTION SAYS IT WILL HAVE A TRULY USEFUL QUANTUM COMPUTER BY 2028

Quantum computers are built from qubits. Most qubits make a lot of mistakes. To fix that, companies group several of them together into one reliable "logical qubit." Logical qubits are the ones that actually matter.

Infleqtion just built 30 logical qubits using only 80 regular ones, per Forbes. Most approaches need far more raw qubits to get there.

Its goal is 100 logical qubits by 2028. That's around the point where quantum computers could start solving problems no regular computer can.

The trick is how it builds them. Infleqtion uses individual atoms held in place by lasers, and every atom can talk to every other atom. Most big players use superconducting chips that need giant freezers and can only connect neighbors.

Those chips are faster, but they need way more steps to do the same work. CTO Pranav Gokhale says that shrinks their speed edge from about 1,000x to about 10x.

"What really matters is if we get to 100 logical qubits near-term as planned. I think that will be a challenge for superconducting systems."

It's already making money too, selling ultra-precise atomic clocks and sensors. It raised more than $500M in its IPO this year and expects about $45M in revenue in 2026.

What's next for AI? 

@ajassy thinks the biggest wave is just getting started in the workloads companies run every day, and bringing down the cost of inference is a big part of unlocking it.

quoted.text:
AI demand is a barbell, with the labs on one end and enterprise cost-cutting on the other. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy says the biggest market sits in the middle, and inference is still "an order of magnitude too expensive" to reach it.

"On one end of the barbell are the AI labs who are consuming gobs and gobs of compute, unlike anything I've seen. And then a few runaway apps, ChatGPT, Claude Code, things like that."

"On the other end of the barbell are enterprises who are largely using AI for cost avoidance and productivity, so automating customer service or fraud or business process automation."

"In the middle of the barbell are the current production workloads of enterprises, many of which are using AWS and using inference today, but I would say the overwhelming majority of which still aren't in any pervasive way."

"And that I think is gonna be the largest absolute segment of AI usage."

"The cost of inference has come down quite a bit in the last few years, but it's still an order of magnitude too expensive, in my opinion, for it to be used as pervasively as possible."

"If you're asking enterprises to rewrite their applications that use CPU today with AI accelerators... the amount of incremental benefit they have to get is a much higher bar to want to rewrite those apps. But if you can take the cost of inference down, that bar is much lower, and all applications are gonna be better and smarter and more capable."

Today’s GPT-6 Cyber release is a meaningful step for defenders: stronger vulnerability research and better alignment. We’ve already been using GPT-6 Cyber alongside GPT-6 Astra with Daybreak to harden our own systems, finding weaknesses, validating their impact, and developing fixes.

Even after years @OpenAI, model capabilities continue to surprise me. One small example came from testing a prerelease version of GPT-6 Astra earlier this summer. We were examining tools used across our research infrastructure and one of our research infra leads, Michael Dalton, was looking into some low risk areas like a math task grader that used SymPy, a mathematics library, to check answers.

In an offline test, the submitted answer used characters that looked like ordinary letters to get past the grader’s checks. It caused the grader to run a shell command that printed “4242”, while still returning the expected result, 1/2. The grader marked the answer correct. A valid math answer had become a way to run code inside the grader - diagram below.

This is the kind of vulnerability that can be very hard for a human to find, even with a fuzzer. It takes connecting how input validation and evaluation interact, constructing an input that passes the checks but triggers unintended behavior, and recognizing the failure even when the final answer is correct. Models can reason across those pieces and help uncover classes of vulnerabilities that are difficult to spot when reviewing components in isolation.

That’s why it’s important for more defenders to use models with Daybreak to find and fix vulnerabilities in their own systems. Whether it’s a potentially internet-melting bug like PHP2Shell or a subtle but important issue like this grader bug, finding it before an attacker does gives defenders time to act.

Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers.

We’re also expanding Daybreak Blue alpha access for GPT‑6 Astra to more organizations and individual security researchers - let us know if you’re interested:

posts.text:
Let's put all this AI fear mongering in perspective because there's a real chance the narrative does more damage than the evidence supports. So, where's it actually hurting or is it? 

Jobs: very little aggregate damage so far. A Stanford SIEPR review found that the unemployment rate for AI-exposed workers had risen 0.77% since 2022, while the rate for the least-exposed workers went up 0.85% over the same period. There's only thin evidence that AI is hurting labor so far. IMO robotics is the place where we need to be careful so overregulating the software and data center buildout seems misguided. 

Electricity: a more legitimate gripe, but the evidence is mixed. Electricity prices are up 4.5% YoY and have been sticky ever since Covid. Much of that is data center capacity and estimates from Goldman say AI could be causing upwards of 1/3rd of the increase. Even so, this isn't the main cause of high recent CPI, oil and gas is. 

Macro: AI is propping up growth, not hurting it. ING estimated AI and tech investment accounted for 36%+ of US GDP growth in Q2 2026. The AI capex boom is the reason GDP has been strong in recent years. 

On the whole I don't see the evidence of this big bad AI impact and IMO politicians should tread very carefully about overstepping here. Narratives are more powerful than evidence and the evidence so far doesn't support the negative narrative.

One of the most likely catalysts is growing concern about a potential "ban" on AI, or at the very least, severe regulation of the industry.

Over the last 24 hours, Democratic lawmakers have publicly called for restrictions on advanced AI development, including an outright "ban on artificial superintelligence."

Frankly, an outright ban will not happen.

Such a ban, if even possible to enforce, would effectively mean the US surrendering its position in the global AI race to China.

Does this mean AI is "over" or today's stock market crash marks "the end?" Absolutely not.

Rather, we believe we are witnessing a sudden shift in sentiment colliding with excessive levels of leverage, potentially triggering forced liquidations by several major institutional investors.

Therefore, today's downturn is more technical than fundamental. This is not to discount the concerns around regulation, they are legitimate. But price action right now does not look orderly or rational.

We are in the midst of the biggest technological revolution in human history.

There is a generalization here that is worth considering:

While public markets can be fickle, they can also be exuberant. Being public allows the smart capital allocator to generate a warchest balance sheet during heady times and deploy it during contractions. It’s possible to employ the same tactic as a private company but it is much harder. 

The value of being public is access to capital. Simply put. And it turns out capital, when you have a lot of it, solves many problems:

1) employee comp - pay more
2) product - buy defensively 
3) R&D - buy proactively 
4) competition - subsidize to grow
5) growth - consolidate markets  

At the limit, as a tech company, you are always one turn of innovation away from irrelevance. Your cash flows. As a result, are fragile. So being private underprices those cash flows in periods of exuberance and overprices them in periods of meandering or decline. 

It’s a hard trade to make work over a long time horizon.

BUT the idea that the election cycle is actually going to hold over actual fundamentals/current market structure is reckless. This type of seasonality is a fade (e.g. I remember coming into 24 the consensus expected a "weak H1, strong H2" based on election seasonality...that was an obvious fade).
